title: "Consensus ADMM under differential privacy"
subtitle: "When the noise breaks the stopping rule rather than the search"

```{python}
#| include: false
import os

os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "2")
```

::: {.callout-important}
## A demonstration, not a recommendation

The threshold-FHE protocol in [consensus ADMM](consensus-admm.qmd) is
*lossless*: it releases the exact consensus average and leaks nothing
else. Differential privacy releases a deliberately corrupted average,
to bound what repeated releases can reveal. This page shows what that
costs. It is not advice to add it.
:::

## Why this is not the Cox page again

[Cox regression under DP](dp.qmd) adds Gaussian noise to a scalar
objective and watches an optimizer fail. The failure there is in the
*search*: a finite-difference gradient divides noise by a tiny step,
the gradient direction becomes meaningless, and the fit collapses to
its starting point.

Consensus ADMM has a different shape. Nothing is probing an objective.
The only quantity crossing the site boundary is a per-iteration average
of the $x_i + u_i$ vectors, and the iteration is a fixed-point
recursion rather than a search. So the search cannot break — there is
no search.

What breaks instead is the **stopping rule**, and it breaks in a way
that is easy to miss because the loop still returns an answer.

## The mechanism

Unchanged from the Cox page in substance. Site $i$ adds a draw
$\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 N)$ to its $x_i + u_i$ vector *before*
encrypting. The encrypted draws sum under the joint key and the $1/N$
scaling contracts the variance back to $\sigma^2$ per coordinate, so
the recovered consensus carries exactly the intended noise per
coordinate and no party ever holds the clean value — an aggregator that
is compromised sees encrypted, already-noised contributions.

The variance bookkeeping is the only thing that differs from the scalar
case: there the per-site scale is $\sigma/\sqrt{N}$ because the sum of
$N$ draws is released directly; here it is $\sigma\sqrt{N}$ because the
sum is *divided by* $N$ before release. Both land the released quantity
at $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$.

## The stopping rule has to change

ADMM normally halts when the primal and dual residuals fall below a
tolerance. Under noise they cannot. Each iteration re-injects a fresh
draw, so the residuals do not shrink towards zero — they settle onto a
floor set by $\sigma$.

A tolerance test against that floor has two outcomes, and both are bad.
If the tolerance sits below the floor it never fires and the loop runs
to its iteration cap. If it sits near the floor it fires when one draw
happens to land small, which is *worse*, because a lucky draw is
indistinguishable from convergence in the output.

So the loop runs a **fixed** number of iterations instead, taken from
the noiseless fit on the same cohort. The shared ADMM loop already
accepts a tolerance argument, so this needs no new code path: passing
`tol=0.0` disables the early exit and leaves everything else identical.

```{python}
from homomorphepy.examples.dp import consensus_sweep

rows = consensus_sweep()
T, rho = rows[0].n_iter, rows[0].rho
T, rho
```

`{python} T` iterations at $\rho =$ `{python} rho`, both inherited from
the lossless fit rather than tuned under noise — tuning them against a
noisy objective would be the same mistake one level up.

## The sweep

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd

pd.DataFrame({
    "sigma":             [r.sigma for r in rows],
    "max|vs noiseless|": [r.max_abs_vs_noiseless for r in rows],
    "primal residual":   [r.final_primal for r in rows],
    "dual residual":     [r.final_dual for r in rows],
})
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
from IPython.display import Markdown

noisy = [r for r in rows if r.sigma > 0]
err_ratio = noisy[-1].max_abs_vs_noiseless / noisy[0].max_abs_vs_noiseless
sig_ratio = noisy[-1].sigma / noisy[0].sigma
res_ratio = noisy[-1].final_primal / noisy[0].final_primal
Markdown(
    f"Across the noisy rows, sigma rises {sig_ratio:.0f}-fold, the "
    f"coefficient error rises {err_ratio:.0f}-fold, and the primal "
    f"residual rises {res_ratio:.0f}-fold."
)
```

The coefficient error grows **linearly** in $\sigma$. That is the
honest price of the mechanism and it is not a surprise.

The residual columns are the interesting ones. They grow linearly too,
which is the noise floor made visible. At the largest $\sigma$ the
primal residual settles at
`{python} f"{noisy[-1].final_primal:.1e}"` and simply stays there — any
tolerance below that would never be met no matter how long the loop
ran. This is the concrete reason the stopping rule is a fixed iteration
count rather than a threshold, and it is measured rather than argued.

## The $\sigma = 0$ control

```{python}
#| echo: false
control = rows[0]
Markdown(
    f"At sigma = 0 the fixed-iteration loop lands within "
    f"{control.max_abs_vs_noiseless:.1e} of the lossless fit, with "
    f"primal residual {control.final_primal:.1e}."
)
```

This row is the control, and it is the reason the rest of the table can
be read as a statement about privacy. Replacing a convergence test with
a fixed iteration count is a change to the *algorithm*, and it could
have moved the answer on its own. With the mechanism switched off it
does not: the loop reproduces the lossless fit to CKKS approximation
error. Whatever the other rows show is therefore the noise, not the
stopping rule.

## The privacy budget

The accounting is the same zero-concentrated DP composition used on the
[Cox page](dp.qmd), with one structural difference in its favor: the
number of releases is not set by an optimizer's appetite. ADMM releases
one consensus vector per iteration, and the iteration count is fixed in
advance, so the budget is **known before the protocol runs** rather
than discovered afterwards.

```{python}
import math

def zcdp_to_epsilon(rho_total, delta=1e-5):
    return rho_total + 2 * math.sqrt(rho_total * math.log(1 / delta))

def budget(n_releases, sigma, delta=1e-5, sensitivity=1.0):
    rho_total = n_releases * (sensitivity / sigma) ** 2 / 2
    return rho_total, zcdp_to_epsilon(rho_total, delta)

pd.DataFrame(
    [(T, s) + budget(T, s) for s in (r.sigma for r in rows) if s > 0],
    columns=["releases", "sigma", "rho total", "epsilon at delta=1e-5"],
)
```

Sensitivity $\Delta = 1$ is a placeholder, as it is throughout these
pages. A defensible sensitivity bound for the consensus vector is a
separate problem: it would need the per-site iterates to be clipped to
a known radius, which changes the optimization problem being solved and
is not attempted here.

The $\varepsilon$ values at the usable end of this table are large. That
is the finding, not a failure of the implementation.

## What this demonstrates

**The same mechanism meets a different protocol and breaks something
else.** Noise on a scalar objective destroys a search direction; noise
on a consensus vector destroys a convergence criterion. Knowing that
DP "costs accuracy" does not tell you which part of your procedure will
stop working.

**The failure is silent by default.** A residual-based loop under noise
still returns a coefficient vector, still reports a residual, and still
looks converged. Nothing raises. The only reason it is visible here is
that the $\sigma = 0$ control was run alongside it.

**The lossless protocol remains the recommendation.** Threshold FHE
releases the exact consensus and leaks nothing beyond it. Everything on
this page is the cost of adding a second, independent privacy notion on
top of a protocol that did not need it to be correct.

## Limitations

**Fixed $T$ is a blunt instrument.** Taking the iteration count from a
noiseless fit assumes such a fit is available on comparable data. In a
deployment where it is not, $T$ has to be chosen a priori, and choosing
it badly costs either accuracy or budget with no signal to tell you
which.

**Sensitivity is unbounded without clipping.** See above; this is the
gap that would have to close first in any real use.

**One cohort, one draw of it.** The mechanism is randomized, so a
specific coefficient here is not a reproducible quantity. What is
stable is the behavior: linear error growth, a residual floor at
$\sigma$, and a $\sigma = 0$ control that reproduces the lossless fit.

**No accounting for the ADMM iterates themselves.** Only the consensus
releases are counted. A site's own $x_i$ never leaves it, but the dual
variable it maintains is a function of every consensus it has seen, and
a full treatment would say so formally.
